pl-l3d18c3-d1e117.summary: States that he merited not only the glory of impassibility and immortality but the gift of the name above every name, to be called God. Yet he had this name before death: the Son of God had it as God from eternity by nature, and as made man from the time of the incarnation by grace.
claims: Christ had the divine name as God by nature and as man by grace.

pl-l3d18c3-d1e123.summary: Cites Augustine: the name was given to the man, not to God, since he had it when only in the form of God; 'therefore God exalted him' shows why (obedience) and in what form, since in the form he was crucified he was exalted and given the name, so that with the form of a servant he is called the only Son of God. This was given him as man that he already had as God. So by grace he received that he, being man or subsisting in the form of a servant, is called and is God.
claims: The name was given to Christ as man.
By grace the man in the form of a servant is God.

pl-l3d18c3-d1e138.summary: Asks whether he merited this, since it was said earlier that that man did not merit so great a good; how then is the name said to be given for his obedience?
claims: Christ did not merit to be God.

pl-l3d18c3-d1e142.summary: Answers by the very frequent scriptural trope by which a thing is said to happen when it becomes known: after the resurrection what was before was made evident, so that men and demons knew. God gave him the manifestation of the name after the resurrection, and he merited it by the obedience of the passion; obeying in suffering, he was exalted in rising, and so the name was made manifest.
claims: Christ merited the manifestation of his name, not the name itself.
Scripture says a thing happens when it becomes known.

pl-l3d18c3-d1e148.summary: Notes the same trope in Mt 28:18, 'all power in heaven and on earth has been given me', not because he first received it then, but because the power he had before was then manifested.
claims: Christ's power was manifested, not first received, after the resurrection.

pl-l3d18c3-d1e154.summary: Reconciles Ambrose, who says the name was given to God, not to the man, with Augustine: they differ on the surface but not in understanding. Ambrose means the natural gift by which the Father, begetting eternally, gave the Son the name above every name, to be God by nature; the Apostle's saying it was given for the obedience of the passion must be read by the trope already explained.
claims: Ambrose refers to the eternal gift of divinity by generation.
Ambrose and Augustine agree in meaning.

pl-l3d18c3.summary: Teaches that Christ also merited the name above every name, to be called God. He had this name before death: as God from eternity by nature, as man from the moment of incarnation by grace. Augustine says it was given to the man, in the form of a servant in which he was crucified. Since he did not merit to be God, the gift is read by the scriptural trope by which something is said to happen when it becomes known: after the resurrection the name was manifested, and he merited this manifestation by obedience, as all power 'was given' him (Mt 28:18). Ambrose's statement that the name was given to God refers to the eternal gift by generation, not contradicting Augustine.
claims: Christ had the name above every name as God by nature and as man by grace.
Christ did not merit to be God.
Christ merited the manifestation of his name by his obedience.
Things are said to happen in Scripture when they become known.
